480.bp: Large knowledge graphs are maps of facts: one thing is connected to another by a named relation, such as a drug treats a disease, a page cites a source, or a product belongs to a category. The systems that store and query these maps have to be tested at large scale, but real large graphs can be private, expensive, changing, or unavailable in the exact size needed for a fair stress test. This paper serves that practical need: make artificial knowledge graphs that are large enough for testing while still behaving like real ones. The important point is that realism is not only about producing many individual facts. Real graphs have repeated shapes, clusters, dense pockets, and group patterns. SimplexKG asks whether a generator should copy those larger shapes, not just copy the rate at which individual triples appear.
480.wh: The hard part is that a knowledge graph is more than a bag of triples. A triple is one fact with three pieces: a subject, a relation, and an object. If a generator only learns how often those small facts occur, it can create a graph that looks plausible one line at a time but wrong as a whole. Query engines and graph-processing systems are stressed by neighborhoods, connected groups, and repeated structures, not just by isolated statements. A fake graph may have the right number of facts and relation labels while missing the higher-order organization that makes real queries easy or hard. The abstract says current data-driven generators based on versioned datasets are promising, but they work at the triple level. That creates the central tension: synthetic data must be flexible in size, yet must preserve structure large enough to affect downstream storage and query behavior.
480.naive: A smart beginner would take an existing knowledge graph, count its entities, relation types, and triples, then sample new triples with similar frequencies. They might also copy changes from versioned datasets so the artificial graph grows in a realistic-looking way. This would be simple and scalable. It fails because the sampled triples do not know which groups of facts usually appear together. For example, several entities may form a tightly connected domain-specific pattern, and a query engine may rely on that pattern when joining facts. If the generator scatters the pieces independently, the local lines look reasonable but the graph loses its larger shape. The result can mislead a benchmark: the system being tested is no longer facing the same structural workload.
480.ap: The core idea of SimplexKG is to look for connected shapes made from more than one relation before generating the new graph. The paper calls these shapes d-dimensional simplices. In plain terms, a simplex is a small group pattern whose members are connected tightly enough that the group itself matters, not just the separate pairwise links. SimplexKG analyzes these higher-dimensional structures inside an input knowledge graph, treats the collection of such structures as a simplicial network, and uses that network as the pattern source for producing a synthetic graph of arbitrary size. The move is mechanical: preserve the way facts gather into higher-order shapes, then generate new triples through that preserved group structure. The paper tests whether this added structure makes the output more realistic by checking both graph structure and practical utility in triple-store benchmarking.
480.mech: The mechanism begins with an input knowledge graph. At the lowest level, the graph contains triples, each saying that one entity has a relation to another. Instead of stopping there, SimplexKG searches for d-dimensional simplices inside the graph. The abstract does not spell out the exact enumeration rule, but the intended object is clear: a higher-order connected pattern that captures how several facts or entities participate together. After finding these patterns, the method builds a simplicial network, which is a map of these group shapes and how they sit inside the original graph. Generation then uses that learned map as the template. To make a synthetic graph, SimplexKG does not merely ask which single triple should come next. It asks what kinds of higher-order neighborhoods should exist and then fills a graph so those neighborhoods appear at the requested size. The output is a synthetic knowledge graph, meaning a new set of entities, relation labels, and triples whose size can be chosen by the user. The paper evaluates two kinds of output quality. Structural fidelity asks whether the artificial graph has graph-shape properties close to the target. Utility asks whether the graph behaves similarly when used in triple-store benchmarking, where storage systems answer graph queries and throughput error measures how far the synthetic workload is from the target workload.
480.math: The main mathematical idea is graph structure beyond pairs. A normal graph records pairwise connections: this entity is linked to that entity. A knowledge graph triple is a labeled version of that idea. A simplex extends the view from pair links to group shapes. Instead of treating a triangle or a dense local pocket as several unrelated edges, it treats the group as a unit worth counting and reproducing. The dimension d is a way to say how large or complex the group pattern is. This matters because many real systems are affected by group organization: clustered facts create different query paths and storage behavior than the same number of scattered facts. The second idea is generative modeling, meaning learning a rule from an observed object and using that rule to produce a new object. Here the rule is not just the frequency of relation labels but the arrangement of higher-order graph shapes. The evaluation also uses closeness measurements. Structural fidelity compresses graph similarity into numbers, such as the structuredness value mentioned in the abstract. That compression is useful because two large graphs cannot be compared by eye, but it also loses detail: one score cannot reveal every rare pattern. The tradeoff is flexibility versus faithfulness: generate any desired size while keeping enough real structure to be a valid benchmark.
480.dots: This paper sits inside the knowledge-graph family because it treats connected facts as the real object of interest. The repo's current family description frames knowledge-graph work as structured evidence movement: facts constrain neighboring facts, and useful information often appears in paths, neighborhoods, relation types, and missing links. SimplexKG addresses a supporting problem for that whole family. If researchers need to test graph question answering, rule mining, graph storage, crawling, or completion systems, they need large graphs whose connected structure is believable. The paper also connects to graph analytics in the same batch, where gid 481 studies cohesive subgraphs: both care about dense local structure rather than isolated edges. It connects to web crawling and retrieval work through the shared pressure of scale: systems must be evaluated under large workloads without losing the shape of real connected data. Its special contribution is not answering over a graph, but manufacturing a graph that preserves the structural pressures other systems must handle.
480.ww: The approach should work better than triple-level generation when higher-order structure is what makes real knowledge graphs distinctive. If real facts arrive in groups, then independent triple generation breaks the dependency among those facts. SimplexKG instead measures the group shapes first, so the generated graph has a better chance of reproducing the same neighborhoods, dense regions, and structural regularities. That is why the abstract reports improvements in both structural fidelity and triple-store benchmarking. These two checks matter together. A graph could look statistically similar but still create unrealistic query workloads; it could also stress a storage system similarly while hiding structural mistakes. By using simplicial networks as the generation source, the method keeps a middle layer between individual facts and the whole graph. That middle layer is exactly where many graph behaviors live: local clusters, repeated multi-entity patterns, and the arrangement of facts that query engines have to traverse. The causal intuition is simple: preserving the shapes that systems actually touch during processing makes the synthetic graph a more faithful substitute for the target.
480.po: The payoff is a generator for large synthetic knowledge graphs of arbitrary size that better resemble target graphs than the compared alternatives in the paper's tests. The abstract says SimplexKG outperforms two baseline generators and six variants of LEMMING across three datasets. It reports structuralness values up to 26.62 percent closer to the target graph than the second-best approach, and query throughput error reduced by up to 6.59 percent across storage solutions. In practical terms, this gives graph-system builders better benchmark data: large enough to stress processing systems, but less likely to erase the higher-order graph shapes that affect real storage and querying.
480.limits: The abstract supports the claim that higher-dimensional structures help on the tested datasets and triple-store scenarios, but it does not prove the generator preserves every property needed by every graph application. The method assumes the input graph contains useful simplicial patterns and that those patterns are stable enough to reuse when scaling to another size. If rare relations, time evolution, schema constraints, or domain-specific rules matter more than the measured simplices, the synthetic graph may still be misleading. The evaluation covers three datasets and selected storage solutions; broader domains could reveal different failures. Also, structural closeness scores and throughput error are summaries, so they may hide mistakes in small but important parts of the graph.

481.bp: Many network questions start with a simple human idea: find the groups whose members are tightly connected to one another. In a social graph, that might be a community where many people know each other. In a biological graph, it might be a set of genes or proteins that interact often enough to suggest a shared role. In a web graph, it might be a dense pocket of pages or accounts. Perfect cliques, where every possible link inside the group exists, are usually too strict for real data because observations are missing and real systems are noisy. This paper studies a looser target: a maximum edge-based gamma-quasi-clique, meaning the largest subgraph whose internal link count is high enough relative to the number of links it could contain. The practical need is exact dense-group discovery at large scale, where the answer should satisfy a clear density rule rather than merely look clustered.
481.wh: The difficulty is not just that the graph is large. The search space is the set of possible groups of vertices, and that set grows explosively as the graph grows. The abstract says the exact problem is NP-hard, which means no generally fast algorithm is known and worst cases can force an enormous search. A second difficulty is more specific: the edge-based quasi-clique condition lacks the hereditary property. A property is hereditary when every smaller piece of a valid group is also valid. Many graph searches use that fact to prune: if a partial group already violates the rule, all larger or related branches can be discarded safely. Here that safety net is missing. A group that is not dense enough now might become dense enough after adding the right vertices and edges, so ordinary pruning can throw away a path that later becomes the best answer.
481.naive: A smart beginner might try to enumerate candidate vertex sets, count the links inside each set, compute its density, and keep the largest set above the gamma threshold. That is faithful to the definition, but it collapses under scale because there are far too many candidate groups. Another beginner might borrow pruning rules from clique search: once a partial group fails a density test, stop exploring it. The abstract explains why that is unsafe for this model. The edge-based quasi-clique rule is not hereditary, so failure in a partial group does not prove failure after later additions. A simple greedy method, such as repeatedly adding the vertex with many connections to the current group, is faster but can miss the exact maximum.
481.ap: The paper's central move is to change the shape of the search without changing the final target. Instead of attacking one non-hereditary problem directly, it reformulates the task as a sequence of subproblems that do have a hereditary structure. That matters because hereditary subproblems support the classic branch-and-prune discipline: once a branch cannot lead to a valid or better answer under that subproblem's rule, the algorithm can stop spending time there. The method is iterative, so the algorithm repeatedly solves or narrows these better-behaved pieces while moving toward the original maximum edge-based quasi-clique. The authors also redesign the iteration and add a heuristic, meaning a rule for choosing promising search directions based on partial evidence. The result, EQC-Pro, is presented as both theoretically tighter in worst-case time and practically faster on real graphs.
481.mech: The input is a graph, a density threshold gamma, and the goal of returning the largest vertex set whose internal edges satisfy the edge-based quasi-clique requirement. The mechanism begins by treating the original search as too awkward for direct pruning because partial candidates do not preserve the key property. It then builds an iterative sequence of related subproblems where the needed condition is hereditary. In each subproblem, the algorithm can inspect a candidate region of the graph, keep track of the best valid dense group found so far, and compute whether an unfinished branch still has any chance of beating that best group. If the hereditary rule says a branch cannot recover, the branch is removed from the search. Reduction rules can also shrink the graph or candidate set by deleting vertices or edges that cannot participate in a winning answer under the current subproblem. The iteration links these subproblems so progress in one stage tightens the next stage. The redesigned process controls the order and amount of this repeated work, while the heuristic pushes attention toward graph regions that appear more likely to contain dense groups. The output is an exact maximum edge-based quasi-clique, with the abstract claiming better worst-case time complexity than prior approaches and much faster execution in experiments.
481.math: The basic mathematical object is a graph: vertices are entities and edges are observed relationships. A subgraph is a chosen subset of vertices together with the edges among them. Edge density is a ratio: how many internal edges the chosen group actually has compared with how many it could have if every pair were connected. The gamma threshold turns the vague phrase tightly connected into a rule: accept the group only if that ratio is high enough. The maximum version adds a sorting objective, choosing the largest acceptable group. The hard combinatorial part is that the algorithm is choosing from many possible subsets, not adjusting one number. NP-hardness names this explosive worst-case choice problem. Heredity is the key structural idea. If a property always survives when vertices are removed, then failure can be used as proof that whole branches of search are hopeless. This paper's math move is to introduce a sequence of hereditary subproblems so the original non-hereditary target can be reached through smaller rule systems where pruning is logically justified. The tradeoff is exactness versus cost: the algorithm wants the true maximum, but it must avoid checking almost every group. Heuristics add another tradeoff: they guide the search toward likely answers, while correctness still depends on the exact pruning and reformulation rules rather than on guesswork alone.
481.dots: This paper belongs to the repo's graph-learning and graph-analytics family because it asks how useful evidence should be extracted from links rather than from isolated records. Many neighboring papers use graphs to pass signals between nodes for recommendation, retrieval, anomaly detection, or language-model grounding. This one is more algorithmic: it asks how to find a dense structure exactly when the graph is too large for direct search. It connects to the efficiency and scalability theme because the scarce resource is search time, and the central problem is avoiding work without losing the right answer. It also connects to similarity and ranking: density is a particular way of saying that vertices are close as a group, and maximum size defines which valid group is better. The repo also contains a SIGIR 2026 paper on gamma-quasi-cliques for cohesive group discovery in recommender interaction graphs. That sibling emphasizes practical candidate localization under explicit density constraints, while this paper emphasizes exact maximum search through hereditary subproblems.
481.ww: The approach should help because it restores a missing logical handle. In direct edge-based quasi-clique search, a partial candidate can look bad before later additions make it dense, so the algorithm has little proof that a branch is hopeless. By translating the work into hereditary subproblems, the method creates situations where local failure really does imply broader failure. That lets pruning become evidence-based instead of merely hopeful. Every pruned branch saves not just one check but all the descendant groups that would have grown from it, so even small pruning improvements can matter greatly in a combinatorial search. Reduction rules add a second source of savings by removing graph material that cannot affect the final maximum under the current stage. The redesigned iteration matters because a good sequence of subproblems can make later stages smaller and better bounded. The heuristic contributes practical speed by visiting promising dense regions early; strong early answers raise the bar, which gives the pruning tests more power.
481.po: The payoff is a faster exact tool for finding large cohesive subgraphs in complex networks. The abstract names biological, social, and web graphs as settings where such groups help analysts understand structure. It claims EQC-Pro improves worst-case time complexity and outperforms QClique and FPCE by up to four orders of magnitude on 253 large real-world graphs. In practical terms, that means a density rule that was mathematically clear but computationally awkward becomes more usable on large graph collections. The paper also preserves the value of the edge-based gamma-quasi-clique model: flexible dense groups rather than unrealistically perfect cliques.
481.limits: The abstract supports the high-level mechanism but does not give the exact reformulation, pruning tests, heuristic rule, datasets, or parameter settings. The claims therefore depend on the paper's full proofs and experiments, not on the abstract alone. The method assumes the chosen gamma threshold captures meaningful cohesion in the target graph; a bad threshold can return groups that are too loose or too small. It also assumes density is the right signal. Dense links can reflect noise, popularity, duplication, or measurement bias rather than a real community. The speed claims are grounded in 253 real graphs, but the abstract does not prove the same gains for every graph family or for changing, streamed, or adversarial networks.

482.bp: Many web and health systems keep records that are not just rows in a table, but streams of dated events. A shopper views, carts, and buys; a social user posts, replies, and follows; a patient receives tests, visits, and treatments. The useful question is often what event may come next, when it may happen, and which earlier events help explain that risk or choice. EIAN serves this setting. It treats an event history as several interacting timelines, because one kind of event may follow its own rhythm while also being pushed by other kinds. The paper is needed because existing event models sit between two unsatisfying choices. Older point process models are understandable but often too rigid for messy real streams. Neural point processes are more flexible, but they often hide the interaction pattern inside learned machinery. EIAN tries to keep flexibility while making the event-to-event influence more explicit.
482.wh: The hard part is that an event stream has two kinds of structure at once. First, each event type has its own timing habit. Purchases, replies, medical visits, or alarms may recur at different speeds and with different memory. Second, different event types can affect one another. A product view may raise the chance of a later purchase; a social post may trigger comments; one clinical observation may change the timing of another. A simple model that assumes one fixed timing rule for all cases misses this variety. A flexible neural model can fit many patterns, but if it only compresses the whole past into an implicit internal state, the model may predict well without showing which same-type or cross-type interactions mattered. Irregular gaps make this worse. Two events separated by minutes should not always carry the same meaning as the same two events separated by months.
482.naive: A smart beginner might start with a Poisson-style counting rule: estimate how often each event type usually occurs, then predict future events from those average rates. A slightly smarter version would use a Hawkes-style idea, where a recent event temporarily raises the chance of related later events. These are useful starting points because they make time and influence visible. They fail when the shape of influence is not fixed in advance. Real e-commerce, social, and healthcare streams may have event types with different rhythms, delayed effects, and interactions that change across context. Another beginner might use a general neural sequence model. That gains flexibility, but it can bury the important event interactions instead of exposing them.
482.ap: EIAN's central move is to split event modeling into two explicit jobs. One job stays inside each event type and learns how that type behaves over time. This is the intra-type temporal encoder: it preserves the unique rhythm of, say, repeated purchases or repeated visits instead of mixing every event into one timeline too early. The second job looks across event types and asks how one type helps explain another. This is the cross-type interaction decoder: it makes relationships between different event kinds part of the prediction process rather than a hidden side effect. The paper also adds two ways of representing time gaps inside the cross-type step, because irregular spacing is not a nuisance to remove; it is evidence. The result is a model meant to predict future events while also showing which interactions it used.
482.mech: The mechanism starts with an event sequence. Each event carries at least a type and a time, and the time gaps between neighboring events can be uneven. First, EIAN separates the history by event type and sends each type-specific subsequence through an intra-type temporal encoder. This produces a learned summary for each type's own temporal behavior: how that kind of event tends to repeat, fade, or cluster over time. Second, the model brings these type-specific summaries into a cross-type interaction decoder. The decoder uses attention, meaning a learned weighting rule that decides which past event types deserve more influence when explaining a target event type. This step does not treat all previous events as equally useful; it highlights the cross-type links the model believes matter. Third, two temporal encoding mechanisms are inserted into that decoder so the weights can depend on irregular time intervals, not only on event order. A close prior event and a distant prior event can therefore be scored differently even if their type labels match. Finally, the model outputs predictions for event modeling, while the highlighted same-type and cross-type relationships provide interpretable evidence about interaction patterns. The abstract reports experiments showing better predictive performance and deeper insight into these patterns.
482.math: The main mathematical object is a marked point process: a record of events placed on a timeline, where each event has a type. In plain terms, the model is estimating a changing chance that different kinds of events will happen next as history accumulates. Classical Poisson models use a simple rate, like an average pace. Hawkes models add self-excitation, meaning one event can temporarily raise the chance of later events. Those ideas are clear but depend on chosen formulas for how influence rises and fades. EIAN keeps the same basic question, but learns the influence pattern from data. The intra-type encoder is a function that turns one event type's past into a compact memory of its rhythm. The cross-type decoder computes weights across event types; this is attention, a comparison rule that assigns larger weight to past signals judged more relevant for the current prediction. Temporal encoding turns time gaps into numbers the model can compare, so elapsed time affects influence. The tradeoff is flexibility versus transparency. EIAN tries to avoid rigid formulas while still exposing which within-type and between-type signals shaped the prediction.
482.dots: This paper sits in the sequence family described in the repo's concept data: the past matters because order and spacing change what the next event means. It is especially close to time-series and spatiotemporal papers that separate slow and fast behavior, because EIAN also refuses to treat all history as one uniform block. Its sibling idea is Mamba Hawkes Process, named in the sequence concept file, which also focuses on irregular events where both event type and time gap shape the next guess. It also connects to interpretability work, because the model is not satisfied with a correct prediction alone; it tries to expose event interaction patterns. The broader field pressure is the same as in recommendation, healthcare monitoring, social behavior modeling, and anomaly detection: systems need to decide which earlier facts still matter now, which links between event types are real enough to trust, and how much old evidence should fade.
482.ww: EIAN should improve over the naive approaches if real event streams contain both private rhythms within each event type and meaningful influence across types. A single average-rate model cannot express that richness. A hand-specified Hawkes-style formula can express influence, but only in the shapes its formula allows. A black-box neural sequence model can learn complicated patterns, but it may mix all evidence into a single internal summary, making it harder to tell whether the prediction came from same-type repetition, cross-type triggering, or timing gaps. EIAN's separation of labor gives the model a better match to the object being modeled. The intra-type encoder protects each type's own timing pattern before cross-type mixing happens. The decoder then compares event types deliberately, so the model can assign influence where the data repeatedly supports it. The temporal encodings matter because influence usually weakens, delays, or changes shape with elapsed time. If the data contains such structure, the model gets a more faithful set of clues than a flat sequence summary.
482.po: The payoff is a more useful event model for domains where event histories drive decisions, including the paper's stated examples of e-commerce, social networks, and healthcare. The abstract claims that EIAN outperforms existing models in predictive performance across extensive experiments. Just as important, it claims to provide deeper insight into event interaction patterns. That second payoff matters because a system owner may need to know whether purchases are being predicted from prior views, whether social actions are linked, or whether clinical event types interact over time. EIAN aims to make those relationships visible while preserving the flexibility of neural point processes.
482.limits: The abstract does not prove that the highlighted interactions are causal; they are learned predictive associations unless the data and study design support stronger claims. EIAN also assumes event types and timestamps are reliable enough that within-type rhythms and cross-type links can be learned. If important events are missing, mislabeled, or observed at inconsistent resolution, the learned interactions may be misleading. The method depends on repeated patterns in historical sequences, so unusual policy changes, platform redesigns, or medical practice shifts could weaken the learned timing rules. The abstract reports extensive experiments, but it does not specify here which datasets, failure cases, or deployment constraints bound the claim.

483.bp: A web crawler is a machine that starts from known web addresses, follows links, and brings back pages so a search, monitoring, or news service can know what exists. In an editorial crawl, the aim is not merely to download many pages. The crawler needs broad coverage, meaning it should find many distinct publications, and freshness, meaning it should find new material early enough to matter. It also has strict limits. Politeness rules prevent hammering sites, and request budgets cap how many starts or page fetches can be spent. URLBank serves the upstream decision before ordinary search ranking happens: which entry points are worth giving crawl budget to today. The paper argues that production crawlers often still depend on manual seed management, where people maintain lists of starting points. That manual habit wastes work on redundant seeds and misses high-yield ones. URLBank replaces that habit with a controller learned from the crawler's own temporal telemetry.
483.wh: The hard part is that a seed's value is not visible from its address alone. Two starting points may look different but lead to the same set of pages, so choosing both spends scarce requests twice for little extra coverage. Another seed may look quiet most of the time but repeatedly reveals new publications early. A crawler also revisits sites in cycles, called revolutions in the abstract, so the system must care about time: which links persist, which disappear, and which entry points keep producing first-seen pages across repeated crawls. A simple count of pages reached can be misleading because it may reward seeds that mostly rediscover already known pages. A simple freshness rule can be misleading if the links are unstable and cannot be counted on later. URLBank must therefore balance coverage, freshness, stability, and efficiency while respecting the same request budget and politeness conditions as the production crawler.
483.naive: A smart beginner would ask human editors or crawl operators to list important site sections, then give each section a roughly fixed amount of crawl attention. If results look poor, they might add more seeds or keep the ones that historically returned many pages. This fails in two concrete ways described by the abstract. First, it oversamples redundant seeds: several starting points can lead to the same content, so the crawler feels busy while adding little new coverage. Second, it misses high-yield seeds that are not obvious to humans but repeatedly expose new publications. The beginner's rule treats seed value as a static property, when the useful evidence is in repeated crawl behavior over time.
483.ap: URLBank's central move is to treat seed selection as a measured allocation problem rather than a hand-maintained list. It reads temporal crawl telemetry: records from past crawler revolutions showing which links appeared, persisted, and led to first-seen publications. From those records it identifies candidate entry points and gives them two interpretable measurements. Stability asks whether links remain present across revolutions, so the crawler is not betting heavily on vanishing paths. Productivity asks how often a candidate leads to publications that had not been seen before. Then URLBank ranks candidates by greedy marginal gain on a shared-credit coverage objective. In plain terms, each seed gets credit for the new coverage it adds beyond what already chosen seeds cover, and overlapping seeds must share credit rather than each claiming the same pages. The system builds a ranked prefix of seeds for a given budget.
483.mech: The mechanism begins with crawl telemetry collected from repeated visits to many sites. Each record says something about links observed during crawler revolutions and about whether following a route produced first-seen publications. URLBank first turns that history into candidate entry points, which are possible seeds the crawler could start from or prioritize. For each candidate, it estimates stability by checking persistence: does the link or route remain available across repeated crawls, or does it appear only briefly? It estimates productivity by measuring the rate at which the candidate leads to new publications, not merely pages already known. Next, the system considers coverage as a shared resource. If two candidates lead to the same publications or overlapping regions of a site, both should not receive full independent credit. The shared-credit objective assigns value to unique or useful coverage while reducing duplicate reward. The ranking then proceeds greedily: choose the candidate that adds the largest extra gain to the current chosen set, update what is already covered, and repeat until the Top-K or budget limit is reached. The output is not just one best seed. It is an ordered list of prefixes, so production can allocate larger or smaller crawl budgets transparently.
483.math: The main mathematical object is a temporal link graph. The nodes are web locations or pages, the links are observed connections between them, and time matters because the same link can persist, disappear, or newly appear across crawler revolutions. Graph reasoning fits because a seed's value comes from where its outgoing paths lead, not just from the seed's own address. The second idea is estimation from repeated observations. Stability and productivity are not magic labels; they are summaries of history. Stability estimates how often a link remains available over repeated cycles. Productivity estimates how often following a candidate produces first-seen publications. The third idea is ranking under a budget: many candidates exist, but only the top few can receive requests. URLBank converts several measurements into an order. The fourth idea is greedy marginal gain. Greedy means the system repeatedly picks the next candidate with the best immediate extra value. Marginal gain means the value is measured after accounting for what previous picks already covered. Shared credit is the key guardrail: when several seeds reach the same content, their duplicated reach is counted less than unique reach. The tradeoff is speed and interpretability versus perfect global search; the greedy rule is simple, auditable, and practical at web scale.
483.dots: This paper connects web crawling to the broader retrieval and ranking family. Search papers usually ask which documents to show after a query; URLBank asks an earlier question, which web entry points should be collected before downstream retrieval is possible. It also connects to efficiency and scalability work because the scarce resource is explicit: polite requests and crawl budget. The system must get more coverage and freshness without spending more requests. Its temporal link graph links it to network reasoning papers, where relationships carry evidence and repeated structure matters. Its use of stability and productivity links it to sequence and temporal information access: the system trusts patterns seen across crawler revolutions, not a frozen snapshot. Finally, its greedy shared-credit objective connects to allocation problems across the conference, where the central move is choosing a small useful subset from a large pile while avoiding duplicate spending. URLBank is therefore a ranking method for upstream attention, not a page relevance method.
483.ww: URLBank should improve over manual seed management because it uses the crawler's own history to expose patterns humans cannot reliably maintain by hand. If a seed repeatedly discovers new publications early, productivity gives it upward pressure. If a seed's links persist across revolutions, stability says the crawler can rely on it. If a seed reaches mostly the same material as another stronger seed, shared credit reduces its apparent value. That last point matters: a crawler budget is wasted not only by bad seeds, but by good-looking seeds that duplicate each other. The greedy marginal-gain loop directly attacks that waste because each new selection is judged against the set already chosen. The method also works operationally because its scores are interpretable. Operators can see which prefixes are ranked for a budget, diagnose health, version policies, and reverse changes if needed. The shadow A/B result over 5,238 sites supports the intuition: under identical conditions, better seed ordering produced higher coverage, greater efficiency, and earlier discovery.
483.po: The payoff is a more disciplined way to spend crawl attention. Under the same production conditions, URLBank reports higher coverage, greater efficiency, and earlier discovery than manual seed curation in a shadow A/B evaluation across 5,238 sites. The abstract also says gains stay stable across Top-K budgets and approach near-complete coverage with far fewer seeds. In deployment with Meltwater's Pulitzer crawler, the ranked prefixes, versioned policies, and health diagnostics make the allocation visible and reversible. That matters in industrial crawling because operators need improvement without turning crawl policy into an opaque black box.
483.limits: The method assumes past crawl telemetry is a useful guide to future crawl value. If a site changes its structure sharply, blocks the crawler, or starts publishing in a new section with no history, stability and productivity may lag behind reality. Shared credit also depends on correctly observing overlap; if telemetry misses paths, duplicate or unique coverage can be misestimated. The abstract reports a large shadow A/B study and production deployment details, but it does not prove behavior on every type of website, adversarial site, language, or news cycle. Greedy marginal gain is practical and interpretable, yet it can miss combinations whose joint value is better than any seed's immediate extra value.

484.bp: The ordinary problem is that people are beginning to use language models as coding partners, not just as autocomplete tools. A model may draft a function, choose an algorithm, or propose a security-sensitive change, and the human reviewer may not immediately see whether the reasoning behind that code was careful. The paper argues that the danger is not only that generated code can fail tests. The deeper danger is that a single model can reason in a narrow, pattern-driven way: it may follow familiar examples, ignore alternative causes, miss unusual inputs, or be steered by adversarial wording. The authors call this cognitive vulnerability. CodeForge is meant to make code generation more like a serious design review before implementation. Instead of trusting one fluent answer, it forces a proposed solution plan to survive competing viewpoints and then asks whether the plan still holds when the problem is deliberately perturbed.
484.wh: Code is unforgiving because a small hidden assumption can become a production bug, a security weakness, or biased behavior. A language model can sound decisive while skipping the very questions a careful engineer would ask: what if the input is empty, what if the order changes, what if the apparent pattern is a coincidence, what if a malicious user shapes the prompt? Standard tests help, but tests usually check examples someone already imagined. The abstract says conventional testing can struggle because the failures are tied to reasoning deficits, not just syntax or missing cases. Multi-agent systems are not automatically enough either. Splitting work into agents can make a workflow faster, but if all agents accept the same hidden premise, the group still inherits the original blindness. The hard part is creating disagreement that is useful: pressure strong enough to expose flaws, but structured enough to refine a plan rather than produce noise.
484.naive: A smart beginner would ask one strong model to write the code, run the visible tests, and maybe ask the same model to review its own answer. That fails because self-review often repeats the same mental path that produced the first answer. The model may defend its original choice instead of truly imagining a different world in which that choice breaks. Another beginner move is to use several agents merely to divide the task: one writes, one documents, one tests. The abstract says such decomposition can improve efficiency, but it does not fundamentally address deficient counterfactual reasoning or adversarial manipulation. The missing ingredient is not more labor. It is a designed conflict over assumptions before the final plan is trusted.
484.ap: The central move is to turn code generation into an adversarial reasoning process. CodeForge assigns three roles to the reasoning stage. The Optimist makes the strongest case for a proposed solution and keeps progress from collapsing into endless doubt. The Pragmatist asks whether the plan is practical, implementable, and likely to satisfy the stated task. The Adversarial Skeptic actively looks for failure modes, misleading premises, and cases where the plan would only appear correct. These roles iteratively cross-examine and refine solution plans until they converge. Then a separate verification module generates counterfactual perturbations, meaning small deliberate changes to the problem situation that ask, in plain terms, whether the plan would still work if an important condition were different. The paper's core idea is that reliability improves when the plan is hardened before code is produced, not merely debugged after the fact.
484.mech: The input is a code-generation request: a problem description, constraints, and whatever examples or requirements the task supplies. CodeForge first works at the level of the solution plan rather than immediately treating the first draft as final code. One agent, the Optimist, proposes or defends a promising path: what the code should compute, what structure it should use, and why that plan fits the request. The Pragmatist examines the same plan from the standpoint of execution: whether the steps are feasible, whether the assumptions match the problem statement, and whether the proposed code would be maintainable and checkable. The Adversarial Skeptic searches for ways the plan can fail: edge cases, biased assumptions, security risks, adversarial prompts, or cases where a pattern-based answer would mistake correlation for correctness. Their comments are not independent summaries; they are a debate in which each round changes the plan. After the agents reach convergence, the verification module creates counterfactual perturbations. These are stress tests of reasoning: change an input condition, flip a boundary case, or imagine a hostile manipulation, then see whether the plan still survives. The output is a final plan, and by implication code generation guided by a plan that has been challenged before acceptance.
484.math: The main mathematical idea is search under constraints. The system is searching through possible solution plans, but it cannot enumerate every possible program. It instead uses structured scoring by roles: one voice rewards fit to the stated task, another rewards practicality, and another penalizes brittleness. This is a form of optimization, meaning the system defines what counts as wrong or risky and repeatedly changes the plan to reduce that wrongness. The debate also uses adversarial reasoning, which is a mathematical pattern familiar from games: one side proposes a move, another side asks what move would defeat it, and a better strategy is one that survives stronger opposition. Counterfactual testing adds another principle: do not ask only what happens in the observed case; ask what would happen if a key condition were changed while the rest of the task stayed recognizable. That is useful for code because correctness is a statement about many possible inputs, not one example. The tradeoff is coverage versus cost. More adversarial rounds can expose more hidden assumptions, but each round spends extra computation and may introduce disagreement that must be resolved.
484.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of code generation, language-model agents, security, and evaluation. It connects to tool-use and agent papers because it treats a language model less like a single answer machine and more like a coordinated system with roles, checks, and a stopping rule. It connects to retrieval and ranking ideas in a looser way: the system must choose which criticism, plan revision, or stress test should matter most, not just produce every possible objection. It also connects to security work because adversarial manipulation is part of the problem, not an afterthought. The paper family context in the repo groups CodeForge with other systems that split software or tool tasks across agents, but CodeForge's distinctive pressure is reasoning quality rather than workflow speed. Its neighboring idea is trustworthy automation: when a model's output can change real software, confidence must come from challenged reasoning, not fluent explanation alone.
484.ww: It works, if it works, because different failures become visible under different questions. A single model asked to solve a task tends to preserve the assumptions that made its first answer seem plausible. A debate changes the information surface. The Optimist must make the positive case explicit, which exposes what the plan depends on. The Pragmatist turns vague elegance into practical checks: can this actually be implemented and validated? The Skeptic supplies pressure that the original model might avoid, especially around adversarial inputs and unusual cases. When the plan changes after these attacks, the system has not merely generated more text; it has moved from an untested story to a plan that has survived targeted objections. The counterfactual verifier then tests the most important claim about code: it should behave correctly across variations, not only on the exact example that inspired it. The abstract reports that removing either adversarial dialogue or counterfactual verification weakens the system, which supports the view that both disagreement and perturbation carry useful signal.
484.po: The payoff is more trustworthy AI-assisted software development. In the full local abstract, evaluations on HumanEval and MBPP, two coding task suites, show CodeForge outperforming prior methods and reaching 97.3 percent pass@1 with GPT-4. The abstract also says ablation studies confirm that both adversarial dialogue and counterfactual verification are necessary. In practical terms, the claimed gain is not just a higher score. It is a shift from passive debugging after a model has committed to code toward proactive hardening of the reasoning plan before the final answer is trusted.
484.limits: The result depends on the debate roles producing genuinely different pressure rather than three versions of the same model habit. If the Optimist, Pragmatist, and Skeptic share the same blind spot, debate can sound rigorous without finding the flaw. The verifier also depends on useful counterfactual perturbations; shallow or irrelevant changes will not reveal deep bugs. The abstract reports benchmark success, but benchmark tasks are still controlled coding problems, not proof that the system catches every production security issue, bias, dependency problem, or ambiguous requirement. Extra debate also costs time and computation, so deployment would need to decide which coding tasks deserve this heavier review.

485.bp: This paper is about stopping harmful network traffic while the traffic is still inside the network, before it reaches the servers or users it is trying to hurt. A network intrusion detection system watches flows of packets, decides whether a flow looks malicious, and can drop it quickly. The practical difficulty is speed. Modern programmable switches can process packets at terabit-per-second rates, so they are attractive places to run detection. But a switch is not a roomy general-purpose computer. It has strict memory, table, and processing limits. Existing systems first train a complex traffic classifier, then convert it into decision trees because trees can be executed as simple step-by-step rules in the switch. Proteus serves the need for a detector that keeps the fast in-network placement, but does not pay for it by either cutting away too much of the tree or copying many large tree structures into scarce switch resources.
485.wh: The hard part is that accuracy and hardware cost pull in opposite directions. A decision tree classifies a flow by asking a sequence of yes-or-no questions about its features, such as whether some measured traffic property crosses a threshold. A rich tree can keep many branches and make finer distinctions between harmless and malicious flows. A programmable switch, however, can only hold and coordinate so much logic. If the system deploys one tree, it often has to prune it, meaning it removes branches until the tree fits. That can erase exactly the branches that catch subtle attacks. If the system deploys multiple trees, it can preserve more decision detail, but now it spends more switch resources and must coordinate among tree replicas. The abstract frames Proteus around this fundamental tradeoff: one small tree is cheap but inaccurate, while several trees are more accurate but expensive and slower to coordinate.
485.naive: A smart beginner would take the trained traffic model, turn it into one decision tree, shrink the tree until it fits the switch, and run every flow through that one compact rule set. This is simple because each packet flow follows one path through one tree and gets one label. It fails when the removed branches were not equally disposable. Some parts of a tree may handle common easy cases, while other parts may protect important attack boundaries. Pruning treats many branches as cost to remove, but Proteus's abstract says different sub-trees have different impacts on overall accuracy. The opposite beginner move is to deploy many tree copies, but that spends scarce switch memory and processing capacity and creates coordination overhead.
485.ap: Proteus's core move is to stop treating the decision tree as one indivisible object. Instead, it splits the original tree into one critical sub-tree and several normal sub-trees. The critical part is the portion whose presence matters most to the final classification accuracy; the normal parts are still needed for full coverage, but they do not all carry the same accuracy value. Once the tree is divided, the system can match these pieces to the available switch resources and the required accuracy target. It then decides how to place and coordinate the pieces so every flow still has a route through the classifier. When switch resources or observed classification accuracy change, Proteus can reallocate or migrate sub-trees instead of rebuilding the whole deployment. The concrete idea is selective preservation: keep the most accuracy-sensitive decision logic close and intact, while arranging the less critical logic in a cheaper way.
485.mech: The input to Proteus is a decision tree produced from a trained malicious-traffic classifier, along with an accuracy requirement and switch resource budgets. First, Proteus analyzes the tree as a set of smaller tree-shaped pieces. It separates one critical sub-tree from several normal sub-trees, using the abstract's stated premise that these pieces have unequal effects on overall accuracy. Second, it must place those pieces on programmable switches. Placement is not just a packing problem, because the pieces still have to work together as one classifier: a flow must enter the correct piece, continue to any needed later piece, and end with a malicious-or-benign decision without losing coverage. Third, Proteus chooses placements that reduce coordination overhead between sub-trees while ensuring full flow coverage. The abstract says this decision is made with mixed-integer linear programming, meaning the system writes the placement choices, resource limits, and coverage requirements as equations and yes-or-no decisions, then searches for an allowed arrangement with low coordination cost. Fourth, Proteus keeps watching the deployed system. It monitors classification accuracy and switch resource changes. If resources shift, it dynamically reallocates or migrates sub-trees, moving pieces rather than accepting stale placement. The output is an in-switch traffic detector that preserves more useful tree structure while using fewer switch resources and reducing classification latency.
485.math: The main mathematical object is a decision tree: a branching set of tests where each internal point asks a question about the flow and each path ends in a class decision. The key insight is that branches are not all equally valuable. Removing one branch may barely change behavior, while removing another may collapse an important boundary between attack traffic and normal traffic. That makes the tree a weighted structure: its parts have different accuracy consequences and different hardware costs. Proteus also uses constrained choice, which is optimization in plain terms: define what must be satisfied, define what should be made small, and search among possible deployments. Here the must-haves are full flow coverage and switch budget limits. The quantity to reduce is coordination overhead between sub-trees. Mixed-integer linear programming is the specific language for this kind of choice. Some decisions are whole-number or yes-or-no, such as whether a sub-tree sits in a particular place; other quantities can be measured linearly, such as resource use or coordination cost added across placements. The method fits because switch deployment is not a matter of gradual guesswork. A sub-tree is placed or not placed, coverage is satisfied or not, and budgets are exceeded or not. The tradeoff is accuracy versus hardware cost, plus speed versus coordination.
485.dots: Proteus connects to the repo's privacy and security family through the shared question of what useful signal can cross a boundary without creating a new risk. In federated and privacy papers, the boundary is often between private data holders and a shared model. Here the boundary is between a rich trained classifier and a constrained network switch. Only some decision logic can fit at line rate, so the system must decide what signal is worth carrying into the switch. It also connects to the optimization concept in the local JSON data: many papers turn a messy operational goal into a measured search over choices under limits. Proteus does that for sub-tree placement, where the choices are constrained by switch resources and by the need to cover every flow. It sits near anomaly and fraud detection work too, because all of these papers ask how to catch harmful behavior without letting normal volume, noise, or scale overwhelm the detector.
485.ww: Proteus should work better than the naive approaches because it uses the uneven value inside the decision tree. If a tree must be made smaller, the important question is not how many branches can be removed, but which branches can be moved or simplified with the least damage. Splitting the tree into critical and normal sub-trees gives the system a way to protect high-impact decision logic while still accounting for the rest of the flow space. The placement step helps because a detector spread across pieces can become slow or wasteful if every classification requires excessive coordination. By explicitly minimizing that coordination while requiring full flow coverage, Proteus aims to avoid a fragmented design that is accurate on paper but costly in the switch. The dynamic reallocation step matters because network devices do not have fixed spare capacity forever. Monitoring both accuracy and switch resource changes lets the system respond when the earlier placement is no longer the best fit. The advantage is therefore not one trick; it is preserving accuracy-sensitive structure, packing it under hard limits, and revising placement as conditions change.
485.po: The payoff is a malicious-traffic detector that can run inside high-speed programmable switches without choosing between an over-pruned single tree and expensive multiple tree replicas. The abstract reports testbed experiments with 12.8 Tbps programmable switches and says Proteus improves classification accuracy, reduces switch resource consumption, and reduces classification latency. In practical terms, it buys earlier blocking of bad flows while keeping the switch fast enough to do its normal packet-processing job. The result is especially useful when security logic must live close to the traffic path, where sending every suspicious flow to slower external machinery would add delay or miss high-speed attacks.
485.limits: The abstract does not prove that every trained model can be usefully converted into a decision tree whose sub-parts have cleanly separable importance. Proteus also depends on accurate measurement of classification accuracy and switch resource changes; bad monitoring would lead to bad migration choices. The mixed-integer placement model is only as faithful as the costs and constraints written into it, so unmodeled switch behavior could weaken the result. The evidence is testbed-based, including 12.8 Tbps switches, but the abstract does not describe all traffic mixes, attack types, or deployment topologies. It also does not show how attackers might adapt once they know which tree parts are critical.

486.bp: Online platforms use toxicity detectors to decide when a comment, post, or message is likely to harm the social space around it. The object is ordinary text, but the decision is not just about spelling. A toxic message can keep its intent while changing its surface: letters are swapped, words are misspelled, spacing is altered, or coded wording is used so that a filter trained yesterday no longer recognizes it. ContiGuard serves the moderation system that must keep reading these disguised messages as the disguise changes over time. The paper treats toxicity detection as an ongoing contest rather than a one-time classification task. A detector is useful only if it can absorb new evasive tricks without losing its older ability. The need comes from a practical asymmetry: malicious users can cheaply invent perturbations, while a platform cannot rebuild and retest its whole detector from scratch every time the spelling of harm changes.
486.wh: The hard part is that the attack changes both the words and the learning problem. If a perturbation merely added harmless noise, a detector could ignore it. But the abstract says perturbation-induced noise distorts semantics, meaning the altered text becomes harder to understand, and it also damages critical feature learning, meaning the detector may start paying attention to the wrong signs. Different perturbations are not interchangeable either. A misspelling, a substitution, and a coded phrase can each damage comprehension in a different way, so examples of one evasion style may not teach the detector how to handle another. Continual learning sounds natural because it updates the detector as new attacks arrive, but continual updates create their own tension. The system must learn the new trick, keep the old toxic clues, avoid becoming sensitive to surface noise, and still make a binary moderation decision from text whose meaning has been intentionally obscured.
486.naive: A smart beginner would train a toxicity detector on normal harmful and non-harmful posts, then add examples of known disguises whenever attackers reveal them. That helps for the exact disguises in the training pile, but it fails as a defense strategy. First, a static detector freezes yesterday's view of evasion and treats tomorrow's perturbation as an unfamiliar writing style. Second, retraining on each new pile of perturbed text can make the model chase accidental surface patterns, such as a particular typo, instead of the harmful intent. Third, learning only the newest attack can weaken memory of older attacks. The naive approach treats perturbations as extra examples. ContiGuard treats them as evolving distortions that must be understood, separated from meaning, and remembered over time.
486.ap: The central move is to make the detector update continually while protecting the meaning signal from the noise introduced by evasion. ContiGuard does this with three linked strategies described in the abstract. First, it enriches perturbed text with possible meaning and toxicity-related clues supplied by a large language model, a system trained to read and generate language patterns from many examples. This tries to restore comprehension before classification. Second, it learns features by discriminability, meaning it strengthens the parts of the representation that separate toxic from non-toxic cases and suppresses parts that do not help make that separation. Third, it replays historical capability by aligning new features with features learned earlier, so the detector does not forget older perturbations while adapting to newer ones. The core idea is not simply to add more data. It is to turn a moving evasion contest into a controlled memory-and-filtering problem.
486.mech: The input is a stream of text examples where some toxic messages have been altered by evasive perturbations that change over time. For each new stage, the system cannot assume that the next perturbation looks like the previous one. ContiGuard first tries to repair the reading step. It asks a large language model to add semantic enrichment: likely meanings and toxicity-related clues that may be hidden by the perturbed wording. The detector therefore receives not only the noisy text surface, but also extra language evidence about what the text may mean and why it may be toxic. Next, the system learns which features are useful for the decision. A feature here is a measurable internal sign extracted from text; it might correspond to a wording pattern, a meaning clue, or a toxicity cue. The discriminability-driven step compares how well these signs separate toxic cases from non-toxic ones. Signs that help draw a clean boundary are amplified, while less helpful signs created by perturbation noise are weakened. Then the continual part handles time. As new perturbation types arrive, the detector updates on them, but it also uses historical capability replay. Instead of letting old detection ability vanish, it aligns current features with earlier learned features, preserving older useful distinctions while adding new ones. The output is an updated toxicity detector meant to classify both current perturbed text and previously seen evasion styles.
486.math: The main mathematics is learning from examples under a moving input stream. Learning means the detector has adjustable settings that turn text into a toxicity decision, then those settings are changed when examples show the decision is wrong or fragile. Continual learning adds memory pressure: the settings must move enough to handle new perturbations, but not so far that they erase old distinctions. That is the stability-versus-adaptation tradeoff. The semantic enrichment step uses language-model probability in plain terms: from many patterns of language, the model estimates what meaning and toxic clues are plausible behind damaged wording. This is not proof of intent; it is an evidence-generating step that can help recover meaning when the surface text is corrupted. The discriminability step is about separation. Imagine placing examples so that toxic and non-toxic cases should fall on different sides of a boundary. Useful features make that separation clearer; noisy features blur it. The method scores features by whether they help separate the classes and changes their influence accordingly. Feature alignment is a memory-preserving comparison: the current detector's internal signs are kept close to earlier useful signs so older capability is not lost. The math fits because the problem is not one fixed rule. It is a repeated balancing act among meaning recovery, class separation, and memory over time.
486.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of text mining, trust, security, and online moderation. Like other text-mining papers in the repo's family analysis, it repairs a mismatch between visible words and the decision being made from them: the harmful signal may be present even when the surface wording has been changed. Like misinformation and trust work, it treats platform safety as an evidence-management problem, where fluent or altered content cannot be trusted by appearance alone. It also neighbors network security work such as malicious traffic detection because both face adaptive adversaries who change surface patterns to evade a detector. The difference is that ContiGuard's object is language, so the defense must preserve meaning while suppressing perturbation noise. It also connects to the broader learning theme: examples are useful only if the system keeps reusable structure and avoids treating each new attack style as a completely separate world.
486.ww: The mechanism should beat the naive approach because it addresses the three places where evasion breaks detection. First, semantic enrichment fights the comprehension failure. If a toxic post has been distorted, adding likely meaning and toxicity clues gives the detector a clearer object to judge than raw corrupted text alone. Second, discriminability-driven feature learning fights the noise failure. Perturbations create many visible changes, but not all changes matter for toxicity. By strengthening signs that separate harmful from harmless cases and suppressing less useful signs, the detector is pushed toward intent-bearing evidence instead of spelling artifacts. Third, historical capability replay fights forgetting. Continual learning often behaves like a worker who learns the newest policy and forgets last month's cases. Aligning new features with earlier useful features gives the update a memory anchor. The result is a detector that can change without treating change as permission to discard what it already knew. That is the right shape for an adversarial language problem where both old and new disguises may appear together.
486.po: The payoff is sustained toxicity detection against evolving evasive perturbations. The abstract says ContiGuard is tailored for continual toxicity detection on time-evolving perturbed text, and that experiments show superior performance over existing detectors and continual methods. In practical terms, the system buys a moderation capability that can be updated as attackers change their disguises, while still trying to preserve older detection ability. It also gives a more specific recipe for the problem than ordinary continual learning: recover likely meaning, prefer discriminative toxicity clues, and replay historical capability through feature alignment.
486.limits: The claims depend on the perturbation stream used in the experiments representing real evasive behavior on platforms. If attackers invent perturbations that the language model cannot interpret, semantic enrichment may add weak or misleading clues. If the labels for toxicity are culturally narrow or inconsistent, better feature separation can still preserve the wrong boundary. Historical replay assumes earlier features were useful and worth keeping; preserving them could also preserve old mistakes. The abstract reports superior experimental performance, but it does not prove long-term deployment behavior, human moderation acceptance, fairness across communities, or resilience against coordinated attackers who adapt after observing ContiGuard itself.

487.bp: The paper is about a workshop, so the real object is not one model but a workbench for a growing kind of Web knowledge. Scientific papers, patents, technical reports, and legal materials are piling up online. People want machines to search them, compare them, extract facts from them, and support decisions with clear evidence. The difficulty is that these sources are not clean rows in a database. A patent may mix claims, formulas, drawings, and tables. A legal document may depend on definitions and cross-references. A scientific article may explain an idea in prose while putting crucial evidence in figures. SemTech 2026 asks how Web systems can turn this mixed material into structured meaning. Its central need is reliability: language models can read text fluently, but scientific, technical, and legal work also needs traceable entities, relations, and reasoning steps.
487.wh: The hard part is that the Web data named in the abstract is heterogeneous and semi-structured. Heterogeneous means the records do not all use the same shape: patents, reports, articles, figures, and tables carry different kinds of evidence. Semi-structured means there is some order, such as sections or table columns, but not enough for a machine to treat every item as a clean database entry. A system that reads only running text can miss the meaning of a table, a figure, or a specialized legal phrase. A system that demands perfectly structured input can ignore most of the useful Web. The tension is therefore between flexible reading and disciplined checking. Natural-language systems can handle messy wording, while Semantic Web tools can represent named things and relationships. The workshop exists because neither side is enough by itself for large scientific, technical, and legal collections.
487.naive: A smart beginner might scrape all the documents, convert them into plain text, and ask a language model to summarize, classify, or answer questions from that text. This sounds attractive because it avoids designing special structure for every source type. It fails because the conversion throws away shape. Tables lose column meaning, figures become captions or disappear, and legal or technical relations may be flattened into sentences that sound clear but are hard to verify. Another beginner might build a strict database schema first. That fails in the opposite direction: the Web sources are too varied, so many facts will not fit the schema without manual repair.
487.ap: The core idea is to make the workshop a meeting point between three ways of handling knowledge. Semantic Web technologies provide explicit records of entities and relations: this patent mentions this chemical, this article cites this method, this legal clause depends on this definition. Natural Language Processing, meaning software that reads and transforms human language, helps pull candidates out of prose. Large language models, meaning systems trained to continue and respond to text, help with flexible interpretation over varied documents. The workshop's key move is to ask how symbolic AI, meaning rule-like and graph-like representations that can be inspected, can work with language models that are powerful but often opaque. The goal is not just better extraction. It is a more reliable pipeline where generated answers can be tied back to structured knowledge and reasoning.
487.mech: The mechanism implied by the abstract can be read as a pipeline for turning messy Web material into usable knowledge. First, the system receives documents from scientific, technical, or legal settings: patents, reports, scholarly papers, tables, and figures. Second, it identifies the pieces that matter, such as named entities, document sections, table cells, visual objects, citations, claims, and relationships between them. Third, language-processing tools interpret the surrounding wording so a phrase is not treated as an isolated string. Fourth, structured representations record what was found in a form a machine can check: entities become nodes, relationships become labeled links, and document evidence remains attached to the claims it supports. Fifth, language models can use this structure when answering, summarizing, or explaining, instead of relying only on fluent text generation. Sixth, reasoning methods can test whether pieces are consistent, whether a proposed answer follows from known relations, and whether a generated explanation points to real source evidence. The output is not merely a paragraph. It is a machine-usable map of technical meaning plus language-based assistance that can be interpreted, inspected, and revised.
487.math: The main mathematical idea is structured representation. In plain language, this means deciding what the important objects are and what kinds of links are allowed between them. A graph is the natural shape: nodes stand for entities such as documents, legal clauses, technical terms, methods, tables, figures, or claims; links stand for relations such as cites, defines, contains, supports, contradicts, or depends on. This fits the problem because scientific, technical, and legal knowledge is not just a bag of words. Meaning often sits in relations. A patent claim matters because of what it covers; a table matters because each number belongs to a row and column; a legal sentence matters because it depends on definitions elsewhere. The second idea is reasoning, which means following allowed links and rules to check whether one claim can be supported by other claims. The third idea is uncertainty: language tools may extract the wrong entity or miss a figure, so confidence must remain visible. The tradeoff is flexibility versus control. Free text handles variety, while structure makes checking possible. The useful number is not only a score; it is a record of what evidence connected to what.
487.dots: This paper connects most directly to the conference's knowledge-graph thread, where the shared problem is that facts need to be connected, not merely stored. The repo's knowledge-graph family explanation frames this as structured evidence movement: decide what the objects and relations are, then let evidence travel only through meaningful links. SemTech sits in that same space, but at the workshop level and with scientific, technical, and legal Web material as the focus. It also connects to the information concept: large collections contain too many signals, so systems must decide which pieces change what is known and deserve attention. Figures, tables, patents, and articles are exactly the kind of mixed evidence where equal treatment fails. Finally, it connects to language-model reliability and retrieval work. The abstract's central bridge between symbolic AI and language models is an attempt to make fluent answers answerable to explicit knowledge.
487.ww: The approach works in principle because each side repairs a weakness in the other. Language models and language-processing tools are useful for messy documents because they can cope with varied wording and incomplete surface structure. But if they operate alone, they may produce an answer that sounds right without showing which entity, table, figure, or legal relation supports it. Structured knowledge does the opposite. It is less flexible at first, but once a fact is placed into a graph or rule-like form, other software can inspect it, follow it, and test it for consistency. Combining them creates a loop: language tools propose meanings from messy sources, structured representations preserve those meanings in checkable form, and reasoning tools ask whether the pieces fit together. That is why the workshop emphasizes interpretability, meaning a human can inspect why an answer was produced, and reliability, meaning the system's output is constrained by recorded evidence rather than only by plausible wording.
487.po: The payoff is a research direction for Web-scale technical knowledge systems that can handle more than ordinary prose. If the workshop succeeds, machines become better at processing patents, technical reports, scholarly articles, figures, and tables as connected evidence. Users could get answers and summaries that are easier to trace back to source objects and relations. The abstract grounds the value in interpretability and reliability: structured knowledge and reasoning can make data-driven language models less of a black box for scientific, technical, and legal work.
487.limits: The abstract describes a workshop agenda, not a completed method with measured results. It does not prove that any specific combination of Semantic Web tools, language processing, and language models works better on a defined dataset. The approach assumes that entities and relations can be extracted from figures, tables, prose, and legal or technical wording with enough accuracy to support reasoning. It also assumes that the chosen structure captures the relations that matter. If the graph is incomplete, stale, or too coarse, reasoning may only make wrong structure look more authoritative.

488.bp: Shared pretrained image models create a practical deletion problem. A model may have absorbed information about a private person, a copyrighted class of images, or a sensitive category before anyone asks for removal. The service owner can make the final classifier stop naming that class, but that is not the same as making the model forget what it has learned internally. This paper serves the people who must audit that difference. The ordinary question is simple: after an unlearning method is applied, is the unwanted knowledge gone, or is it still sitting inside the model where another intervention can bring it back? The paper studies that question for image classification, where a model turns an input picture into internal signals and then into a class decision. Its core contribution is not another forgetting method. It is a test that looks below the final answer and asks whether class-specific internal features can be restored.
488.wh: The hard part is that a model has more than one place to hide knowledge. The visible output is only the final decision. Before that decision, intermediate layers hold many partial signals: shapes, textures, object parts, and class-related patterns that later layers use. A deletion request might change the final boundary that separates one class from another, while leaving those earlier signals largely intact. Output metrics miss this because they ask only whether the model still predicts the forgotten class. A model can pass that test by refusing to say the class name, much like a person who avoids answering while still remembering the fact. For true unlearning, suppression is not enough, because preserved internal features can be recovered by steering the model during use.
